[c368eb88968f0542dc9850a9586c43e9bcb5c1c1503454e5f04c4f297b0c67d7 | https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/6fbbb475-58f1-49e0-90b3-f329e8124694 | page 75]
The societal poverty line, a relative measure of poverty, was developed to capture the shifting nature of deprivation across income levels. Following the recommendations of the Atkinson Commission on Global Poverty (World Bank 2017), the societal poverty line varies according to the living standards in an economy. It is set equal to $1.30, plus half the median consumption or income in the economy, with a floor at the $3.00 international poverty line (Foster et al. 2025) (refer to annex 1A). This (weakly) relative approach reflects a recognition that poverty partly involves exclusion from a normal life in a given society. It also allows the poverty line to be specific to an economy. Globally, the societal poverty line varies with average income in a way that approximately corresponds to the way national poverty lines vary with average income across countries (Foster et al. 2025; Jolliffe

[bfdec343e394de8b039db29cb5cb1f12635c7c961b12aab525be46b997f98bd6 | https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/6fbbb475-58f1-49e0-90b3-f329e8124694 | page 75]
The $3.00 international poverty line measures deprivation with respect to the most basic needs as defined across low-income economies. As an economy’s income level increases, the perception of the composition of these basic needs may evolve (Herforth et al. 2020; Jolliffe and Prydz 2016; World Bank 2024a). Measurement might shift to the application of relative poverty lines that establish the poverty threshold not only according to the requirements to satisfy basic needs, but typically relative to the average level of income or consumption.

[5b44acfbe7485f6eb4153c33d4a2f7d24f9c554b4e856070392cb635445fc7d5 | https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/6fbbb475-58f1-49e0-90b3-f329e8124694 | page 75]
and Prydz 2021).

Regional patterns in societal poverty, as measured by the societal poverty line, mirror the patterns observed in extreme poverty rates. Although the measure is only weakly relative (refer to figure 1.17, panel a), economies with high societal poverty lines tend to exhibit lower societal poverty rates. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for most economies with high societal poverty rates, consistent with the concentration of extreme poverty in the region (refer to figure 1.17, panel b). Higher-income economies typically exhibit lower societal poverty rates, despite their higher societal poverty lines. These comparisons depend on the level of inequality in an economy and, in particular, the concentration of people at the bottom tail (refer to chapter 2).

This is roughly twice the corresponding poverty lines, but with wide variation across economies (Bolch et al. 2026). The threshold also shifts with the risks households face. Those living on between $8.30 and $28.00 a day are above the poverty line of every developing economy and constitute a global middle class; and those above $28.00 a day exceed the prosperity standard this report uses to gauge shared prosperity (refer to chapter 2). results.text: The $3.00 international poverty line measures deprivation with respect to the most basic needs as defined across low-income economies. context_candidates.text: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds Poverty can be described along other dimensions besides poverty thresholds set according to monetary measures of welfare relying on consumption or income. Deprivation can be defined by considering a cutoff determined using basic needs, and it can be defined in relative terms through a comparison among peers. Measurement along nonmonetary dimensions can be useful and revealing.

metadata.section: Poverty extends beyond absolute welfare thresholds

context_candidates.text: The societal poverty line, a relative measure of poverty, was developed to capture the shifting nature of deprivation across income levels. Following the recommendations of the Atkinson Commission on Global Poverty (World Bank 2017), the societal poverty line varies according to the living standards in an economy. It is set equal to $1.30, plus half the median consumption or income in the economy, with a floor at the $3.00 international poverty line (Foster et al. 2025) (refer to annex 1A). This (weakly) relative approach reflects a recognition that poverty partly involves exclusion from a normal life in a given society. It also allows the poverty line to be specific to an economy. Ngưỡng an toàn thay đổi theo nền kinh tế và theo rủi ro hộ gia đình đối mặt: áp dụng phương pháp vulnerability cho khảo sát hộ của World Bank cho ra khoảng 6,00, 7,00 và 14,00 USD/ngày cho ba nhóm thu nhập, gấp khoảng hai lần đường nghèo tương ứng nhưng khác biệt lớn giữa các nền kinh tế; ở Đông Âu và Trung Á, mức cần thiết tăng khoảng 10% thực tế giai đoạn 2008–2018 [42d5e96ebee4eab749b0b04504c045356a3e531dac7bb893ecc6e12763370c22]. Các ngưỡng 3,00–8,30 và 8,30–28,00 USD/ngày chỉ là giá trị xấp xỉ (proxy) để phân loại, không phải ranh giới cố định [a757691789777b49238ff05d33c7598f0e2642ccf8f8ebb73f50a1e4fa16ff9e]; báo cáo cũng cho thấy nhóm 3,00–8,30 USD/ngày gần một phần ba dân số thế giới, nên thoát nghèo cực đoan thường là chuyển sang tình trạng dễ bị tổn thương chứ chưa phải an toàn [38bb5873f8a3883ee4d6957b9cdcf3328407a27227d51d70b44a7ff0edb3d5e1].

Applying the vulnerability approach to the World Bank’s harmonized household surveys—estimating, for each economy, the probability that a household is living on less than the poverty line of the relevant income group over a few years, and identifying the consumption level at which this probability becomes low—yields economic security lines of about $6.00, $7.00, and $14.00 a day for the three income groups. This is roughly twice the corresponding poverty lines, but with wide variation across economies (Bolch et al. 2026). The threshold also shifts with the risks households face. In Europe and Central Asia, the income needed to maintain a low probability of falling into poverty rose by about 10 percent in real terms between 2008 and 2018 as the shocks pushing households into poverty grew larger (Bussolo et al. 2025). There is no fixed income at which security begins. The boundary of the

Measured against these thresholds, the global middle class has grown substantially since 2000, roughly doubling as a share of the world’s population.

The group living on between $3.00 and $8.30 a day, however, has remained close to a third of the world’s population throughout the period. Among large numbers of people, the exit from extreme poverty has thus represented an exit into vulnerability rather than into security.

The thresholds used in this report can serve as approximate class boundaries. Each of the three poverty lines is the typical national poverty line of an income group: $3.00 a day for low-income economies, $4.20 for lower-middle-income economies, and $8.30 for upper-middle-income economies (refer to box 1.1). Households living on less than $3.00 a day are extremely poor by any standard. Those living on between $3.00 and $8.30 are above the extreme poverty line, but would count as poor in a middle-income economy and, for the most part, remain short of economic security. Those living on between $8.30 and $28.00 a day are above the poverty line of every developing economy and constitute a global middle class; and those above $28.00 a day exceed the prosperity standard this report uses to gauge shared prosperity (refer to chapter 2).
